Prefix loss/coalescence and reanalysis of the first member as a lexical predicate intervene between the old finite verb and the modern forms. The final oo of okoó is late-accented: its acute is on the second o. The two-word construction must not be parsed as one inherited finite word.

Their cell differences and come/go semantic organization prevent a direct comparison of old yā́ti with every modern whole word. The linked Kalkoti yuun citation is from Liljegren 2013; Hultman's yùun supplies explicit low-tone evidence associated with lost aspiration, requiring comparison of the same present cell.

The Kohistani báal ‘hair’ versus baál ‘child’ is a particularly clear modern contrast corresponding to vā́la versus bālá. Kalkoti baál is explicitly high-rising in Liljegren 2013 Tables 12–13, a different outcome plausibly associated with loss of the unaccented final vowel found in Palula bóolu.

The linked Kalkoti biš is a segmental citation in Liljegren 2013; tone must be recovered from an explicitly analyzed token or its source context.

analysis: Palula šaák has late accent on old long ā, compatible with final accent in śākhyá after loss of the ending. The parent noun śā́khā has a different accent and must not be substituted silently. Liljegren 2013 analyzes Kalkoti šaàk's falling contour as Low on the second mora, whereas Hultman 2023 analyzes šáak as early High. These are partly alternative phonological analyses of a similar falling pattern, not by themselves evidence of a sound change between 2013 and 2023.
